meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'No act of kindness, no matter how small, is ever wasted'?
meta.ogDescription: The idea is genuinely Aesop’s — but the exact popular wording is a modern paraphrase of the fable’s moral “A kindness is never wasted.”

answer.label: Aesop’s moral — but not in these words
answer.sourceLine: The thought is genuinely Aesop’s: it is the moral of The Lion and the Mouse (Perry Index 150). But this exact sentence appears in no standard translation. The closest documented wording is “A kindness is never wasted,” printed as the moral in the 1919 Aesop for Children; the longer “no matter how small” version is an undated modern paraphrase.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: “A kindness is never wasted” (1919 Aesop for Children)

source.excerpt: “You laughed when I said I would repay you,” said the Mouse. “Now you see that even a Mouse can help a Lion.” Moral: A kindness is never wasted.
trail: Wikiquote’s Aesop page lists the line under general “Quotes” sourced only to “The Lion and the Mouse,” with no translator or edition given.
The Library of Congress’s Aesop for Children (1919) states the moral as “A kindness is never wasted” — the closest documented antecedent.
The scholarly Fables of Aesop collates many translations (Perry 150); none use the popular one-liner, giving morals like “A kindness is never wasted” and “Small causes may produce great results.”
The J. H. Stickney edition on Project Gutenberg gives a wholly different moral — “The weak have their place in the world as truly as the strong” — showing how the wording varies by translator.
source.cutTag: The moral, not a sentence Aesop wrote
source.excerptNote: This is the closing of the fable in the 1919 Aesop for Children. The popular quote — “No act of kindness, no matter how small, is ever wasted” — is a modern expansion of that terse moral, not a line found in any standard translation.

source.rightsNote: The ancient fable is public domain, and the pre-1931 moral “A kindness is never wasted” (1919 Aesop for Children) would itself be public domain. But the exact displayed wording — “No act of kindness, no matter how small, is ever wasted” — is an anonymous modern paraphrase with no identifiable translator and no documented pre-1931 appearance, so we assert no copyright status for it.

author.name: Aesop
author.kicker: The true source of the idea
author.heading: About Aesop
author.bio: Aesop is the name traditionally attached to a large body of ancient Greek fables — short animal tales, each ending in a moral. Whether a single enslaved storyteller of that name lived on Samos in the 6th century BCE is uncertain; the fables were transmitted orally and only written down over centuries by hands such as Phaedrus (Latin) and Babrius (Greek). “The Lion and the Mouse” is among the best-known, and its lesson — that even the smallest creature’s kindness can be repaid — is the true origin of this quote.

misattribution.heading: Right idea, modern words
misattribution.intro: This is less a false attribution than a misquote: the sentiment is genuinely Aesop’s, but the memorable sentence people share is a modern rewording, not a line from any translation of his fables.

items.why: “No act of kindness, no matter how small, is ever wasted” does not appear in the standard translations of “The Lion and the Mouse.” The nearest documented source is the compact moral “A kindness is never wasted” in the 1919 Aesop for Children; the popular line expands it with “no matter how small.”

Aggregators such as Goodreads, BrainyQuote and PassItOn present the sentence as a bare Aesop quotation with no work, translator or date. Even Wikiquote cites only “The Lion and the Mouse” without identifying where these exact English words come from.

misattribution.truthLine: The idea is Aesop’s — it is the moral of The Lion and the Mouse (Perry 150) — but “No act of kindness, no matter how small, is ever wasted” is a modern paraphrase, not a sentence Aesop or his classical translators wrote.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: In the fable, a lion spares a trembling mouse who has stumbled across his paws; later, caught in a hunter’s net, the same lion is freed when the mouse gnaws through the ropes. The story turns on a simple reversal — the powerless creature repays the powerful one — and its moral has been rendered many ways: “A kindness is never wasted,” “Little friends may prove great friends,” “No one is too small to help.”

The modern one-liner distills all of these into a single quotable sentence. That polish is exactly why it reads as a coined aphorism rather than a translation: it is smoother and more absolute than anything in the ancient text, which is the usual fingerprint of a paraphrase.
context.pull: The lesson is ancient; the sentence is modern.
